options.content:
## Viaduct — Fleet Logs
Every node ships journald to Grafana Cloud Loki via Alloy, tagged `node`, `unit` and `level`. Three trust domains, three clouds, one query surface.

**Read it top-down:** pipeline liveness → what the logs cost → the identity and secrets plane (this lab's whole reason to exist) → the data plane → who touched what.

**Deliberately absent:** panels built on `conduit.service` `[STATS]` lines. They are ~96% of the Hetzner node's log volume and duplicate the `conduit_*` Prometheus series — and the log copy is *truncated* (`(+39 more...)`), so `conduit_region_*` is strictly better. Read throughput and per-region breakdown on the ops dashboard; this one shows what those lines **cost** instead.

*Panels scoped to one node (Vault, k3s, egress guardrail) go empty if `$node` excludes it — that is honest, not broken.*

panels.title: Nodes reporting
panels.description: Distinct `node` labels producing lines in the window. Expect 3 (gcp, hetzner, aws). Fewer means an Alloy is down, its credential expired, or the journal group grant was lost — the last of which fails silently, with every component still reporting healthy.

panels.title: Lines shipped
panels.description: Total journald lines across the selected nodes for the dashboard window.

panels.title: Warning and above
panels.description: Lines at journal priority warning/err/crit/alert/emerg. The `level` label comes from `__journal_priority_keyword`, promoted by Alloy's relabel stage.

panels.title: Vault denials
panels.description: Vault audit records carrying a `permission denied` error — a principal reached for something its policy does not grant. Non-zero is not automatically bad (a probing script, a stale token) but every one should be explicable.

targets.expr: sum(count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} |= `permission denied` | json t="type" | t = `response` [$__range]))

panels.title: Break-glass root attempts
panels.description: Calls to `sys/generate-root/*`. This is the documented recovery for re-provisioning Vault and is gated by a 3-of-5 recovery-key threshold held offline — so it is rare, deliberate, and should always correlate with something you were doing. Unexplained, it is an incident.

targets.expr: sum(count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} |= `generate-root` | json p="request.path", t="type" | t = `request` | p =~ `sys/generate-root.*` [$__range]))

panels.title: SSH sessions accepted
panels.description: Successful publickey authentications across the fleet. GCP is reached over IAP, AWS over SSM, Hetzner as a mesh peer — so a login from an unexpected source address is worth a look.

panels.title: Warning and above — the actual lines
panels.description:
Drill-down for the stat above: same selector, so the line count here matches it.

This is journald **priority**, not application severity. A unit that writes its own severity to stdout is tagged `info` by journald no matter what it says, so its warnings appear in that unit's own panel rather than here. What this catches is systemd's own reporting — a crashlooping unit shows up as repeated `<unit>: Failed with result 'exit-code'` from `init.scope`, which is the fastest way to spot one.

panels.title: Line rate by node
panels.description: Lines per second, by node. Grafana Cloud bills on ingested volume, so this is a cost curve as much as an activity curve. A step change with no deployment behind it is usually a service that started retrying.

panels.title: Byte rate by node
panels.description: Bytes per second, using LogQL's `bytes_rate`. Diverging from the line rate above means line *size* changed — verbose JSON audit records weigh far more than a one-line service notice.

panels.title: Heaviest units in window
panels.description: Ranked by bytes, not lines — that is what you pay for. This is the panel that makes a runaway logger obvious. `conduit.service` sitting at the top is expected and is exactly the duplication called out in the header.

targets.expr: topk(15, sum by (node, unit) (bytes_over_time({node=~"$node", unit=~"$unit"} | unit != "" [$__range])))

panels.title: Share of ingested bytes
panels.description: Where the Loki bill actually goes, by unit. Reading this next to the table tells you whether your volume is one loud service or broad-based.

panels.title: Vault requests by principal
panels.description:
Who is talking to Vault. No single audit field names the principal: `auth.metadata.role_name` is the most specific but is set on under half of requests, `auth.display_name` covers most of the rest, and pre-authentication requests (a login itself) legitimately have neither. `label_format` resolves that with a template fallback chain rather than dropping records, so the series add up to the real request rate.

Expect `spire-server` renewing its token continuously, `gcp-viaduct-controlplane` for anything using the box's GCE identity, and `cert-aws-vault-agent` when the AWS Alloy pod starts. A principal you did not deploy, or a familiar one changing rate sharply, is the signal.

targets.expr: sum by (principal) (count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} | json t="type", role="auth.metadata.role_name", disp="auth.display_name" | t = `request` | label_format principal="{{ if .role }}{{ .role }}{{ else if .disp }}{{ .disp }}{{ else }}(unauthenticated){{ end }}" [$__interval]))

panels.title: SPIRE federation heartbeat
panels.description:
Each SPIRE server polling its peer's trust bundle, split by which node did the polling and which trust domain it fetched. Both directions should be continuously present — gcp refreshing `viaduct.aws` and aws refreshing `viaduct.gcp`, roughly every 75s.

**This exists only in logs.** No metric covers federation liveness, so a silent half of this panel is the earliest warning that cross-cloud trust is decaying — well before an SVID actually fails to validate.

targets.expr: sum by (node, trust_domain) (count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit="spire-server.service"} | logfmt | msg = `Bundle refreshed` [$__interval]))

panels.title: Vault paths touched
panels.description: Every secret path reached in the window, with the operation and the role that reached it. This is the audit question — *who read what* — answered directly. `kv/data/*/grafana` is the observability credential; `kv/data/wireguard/peers/*` is mesh registration; `auth/token/renew-self` is routine token upkeep.

targets.expr: topk(20, sum by (path, op, principal) (count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} | json t="type", path="request.path", op="request.operation", role="auth.metadata.role_name", disp="auth.display_name" | t = `request` | path != "" | label_format principal="{{ if .role }}{{ .role }}{{ else if .disp }}{{ .disp }}{{ else }}(unauthenticated){{ end }}" [$__range])))

panels.title: Vault denials
panels.description:
Audit responses carrying `permission denied`, reduced to the four things you want: operation, path, principal, source. `line_format` turns a 2 KB JSON record into one readable line — the full record is still there under the row expander.

A denial is not automatically an attack; it is usually a policy boundary doing its job. The worked example in this deployment: `sys/generate-root/attempt` denied to `gcp-viaduct-controlplane`, because the CWE-863 remediation removed the admin policy's blanket `sys/*` grant. That is the control working — and is exactly what the `enable_unauthenticated_access = ["generate-root"]` listener setting was added to resolve. Denials on `auth/gcp/role/*` are the same story: admin deliberately cannot mint auth roles.

targets.expr: {node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} |= `permission denied` | json t="type", path="request.path", op="request.operation", role="auth.metadata.role_name", disp="auth.display_name", addr="request.remote_address" | t = `response` | label_format principal="{{ if .role }}{{ .role }}{{ else if .disp }}{{ .disp }}{{ else }}(unauthenticated){{ end }}" | line_format "DENIED  {{ .op }} {{ .path }}   principal={{ .principal }}  from={{ .addr }}"

panels.title: Break-glass: root token generation
panels.description: Any call to `sys/generate-root/*`. Regenerating a root token is the documented path for re-provisioning Vault and needs 3 of 5 recovery keys held offline — so this panel should be empty except when you are deliberately doing that. It is given its own panel precisely because it must never scroll past unnoticed in a general log view.

targets.expr: {node=~"$node", unit="vault.service"} |= `generate-root` | json t="type", path="request.path", op="request.operation", addr="request.remote_address" | t = `request` | path =~ `sys/generate-root.*` | line_format "{{ .op }} {{ .path }}  from={{ .addr }}"

panels.title: Conduit lifecycle
panels.description: `conduit.service` with the `[STATS]` firehose filtered out (`!=` on the line), leaving starts, stops, capacity settings and errors. This is the whole reason a line filter beats a unit filter: the useful events are 4% of the stream and invisible without it.

panels.title: Xray, nginx & certbot
panels.description: The rest of the Hetzner ingress path: the proxy, the TLS terminator that fronts XHTTP, and certificate renewal. Certbot is quiet by design — DNS-01 renewals every 60 days — so anything here at all is worth reading.

panels.title: AWS egress guardrail
panels.description: The free-tier cap guard on the AWS node. It reads `aws_mtd_egress_bytes` from the textfile collector and stops the Conduit pod as the monthly cap approaches — so its log is the record of how close you came, and whether it ever actually fired.

panels.title: SPIRE agents & k3s errors
panels.description:
Agent attestation and SVID rotation across both trust domains, plus k3s at error level.

Filters `level_extracted`, not `level`. These units write structured severity to stdout, so journald tags every line priority `info` and the stream label `level` is always "info" regardless; `| logfmt` therefore lands the real severity in `level_extracted`. Measured over one hour: 978 info, 534 warning, 55 error — all with stream `level=info`. Filtering the stream label reads none of them.

panels.title: SSH sessions accepted
panels.description:
Successful publickey logins, with user, source and key type pulled out by a named-capture `regexp` stage and reformatted. Backtick-quoted so the regex needs no escaping.

Expected sources: `35.235.240.0/20` on GCP (that is IAP), the SSM agent on AWS, and your mesh address `10.99.0.4` on Hetzner. Anything else is the finding.

targets.expr: {node=~"$node", unit=~"ssh.*"} |= `Accepted` | regexp `Accepted (?P<method>\S+) for (?P<user>\S+) from (?P<src>\S+) port (?P<sport>\d+)` | line_format "{{ .user }}  <-  {{ .src }}   ({{ .method }})"

panels.title: Rejected SSH by source
panels.description: Failed and invalid-user attempts grouped by source IP. Only Hetzner exposes `:22` at all — GCP and AWS have no public SSH — so this is essentially the internet background noise hitting one host, and it is useful mainly as a baseline you would notice changing.

targets.expr: topk(15, sum by (src) (count_over_time({node=~"$node", unit=~"ssh.*"} |~ `(?i)invalid user|failed password|authentication failure` | regexp `(?P<src>\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)` | src != "" [$__range])))

panels.title: Telemetry pipeline health by node
panels.description:
The panel that would have caught every failure in this deployment. Solid lines are log lines/sec from Loki; the dashed line is the count of healthy Prometheus scrape targets per node. Read the two together:

- **metrics but no logs** -> Alloy is up and scraping, but the log path is broken. Almost always the `alloy` user missing the `systemd-journal` group, which reads zero entries while reporting every component healthy, or a Loki credential that never rendered.
- **logs but no metrics** -> the scrape side. A target moved, or a NetworkPolicy stopped matching it after a namespace change.
- **neither** -> the node or its Alloy is down. On AWS this looked like a Deployment that could never schedule a pod, so nothing logged an error anywhere.

A node whose Alloy has stopped drops out of `up` entirely rather than reporting zero, so watch for a line that *ends* rather than one that falls.

**Read gcp differently.** The control plane is logs-only by design — its Alloy config has no `prometheus.remote_write` at all — so it shows log lines and *zero* scrape targets permanently. That is the one case where the middle rule above does not apply. Only hetzner and aws should ever show a dashed line.

panels.title: AWS egress against the free-tier cap
panels.description:
**AWS only.** The guardrail's whole state in one frame: month-to-date egress, the warn line, the hard cap (all from the textfile collector), and the guardrail unit's own log events on the right axis. The metrics say how close you are; the logs say what the guardrail did about it.

Exceeding the cap is the one thing in this lab that costs real money, so the useful read is the *slope* against the days left in the month, not the absolute value. Log events appearing while the metric is still well under the warn line means the guardrail is evaluating, not acting — which is what you want to see.

panels.title: Probe SLIs against data-plane logs
panels.description:
**Hetzner only** — the probe and the VLESS ingress both live there. The probe's own view of that path: success flag and failure rate broken down by reason — with the error-level log rate from xray and nginx on the right axis.

The correlation is the diagnostic. A probe failure **with** a rise in error-level logs is the service failing and saying so. A probe failure against **silent** logs is the network path between probe and service, or the probe itself — a very different investigation, and one you would waste time on if you only had the SLI.

The log side is the node-wide `level` label (promoted by Alloy from the journal priority), not a parse of xray or nginx. That is deliberate: xray logs `[Info]`-style brackets at journal priority 6 and carries no `level=` key, and nginx's `error_log` is a **file** that never reaches journald at all — so a unit-scoped parser here would be a series that can never fire, which is worse than no panel. Expect silence on this axis most of the time; that is the honest state, and it is what makes a correlated spike meaningful.

panels.title: Conduit: what the metric knows, what the logs cost
panels.description:
Connected clients from `conduit_connected_clients` against the byte rate of `conduit.service`'s own log stream. Both lines describe the same thing; only one of them is worth paying for.

The metric is one sample per 30s with a real `conduit_region_*` breakdown behind it. The log stream is ~0.5 lines/sec of `[STATS]` carrying the same counters, **truncated** at `(+39 more...)`, at roughly 60,000 lines a day. This panel is the argument for why nothing else on this dashboard is built on those lines — and the place you would look first if the Loki bill moved.

panels.title: Fleet log explorer
panels.description: Everything, with all four template variables applied — node, unit, level and a case-insensitive substring. This is the panel you actually drive during an incident; the ones above exist so you know where to point it.
